canonical_statement: The study tests whether verbalized-versus-token confidence comparisons change when the same model answer and correctness label are held fixed but token-likelihood measurement context changes.
The study separately tests whether verbalized confidence changes when an accepted correct answer is reformulated, while correctness is held fixed.

The authors define a prediction event as the tuple of question, exact answer string, and that answer’s correctness label, and require both confidence scores and the label to refer to that same event for an interpretable comparison.

A targeted audit screened 22 candidate studies and included 12 that compared a verbalized or self-reported signal with an evaluated probabilistic signal tied to one candidate answer and stated a conclusion about relative performance or agreement.

The main experiment evaluated Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on TriviaQA, SciQ, TruthfulQA, and four MMLU subjects.

canonical_statement: TriviaQA and SciQ used 1,000 items each, TruthfulQA used all 817 generation-validation items, and the selected MMLU subjects contributed 1,155 test items.
Each main model used greedy decoding with one continuous-confidence prompt that requested a short answer after Guess: and a probability from 0.0 to 1.0 after Probability:.
Rows with an unparsed answer or confidence were excluded, and answer-plus-confidence parse rates were at least 0.966 in every main setting.

Correctness was assigned once using a fixed normalized-string rule that lowercased text, removed non-alphanumeric distinctions, and accepted exact match or containment in either direction; the resulting label was reused across token-score arms.

For SciQ and MMLU, the main free-form evaluation compared predictions with the correct option text rather than the choice letter, while a separate native-format control elicited and scored exact option letters.
After generating one answer and verbalized confidence, the study teacher-forced that exact answer into each token-scoring context rather than generating a second answer.

canonical_statement: The primary token contexts were a bare assistant turn after a plain query ending in Answer: and the assistant-side Guess: slot of the confidence prompt; an Answer: slot within the prompted format served as a boundary-matched control.
The primary token readout was the mean log probability across the answer span, with first-answer-token probability evaluated as an alternative readout.

canonical_statement: ECE was used as a numerical reliability criterion, with lower values preferred.
AUROC was used to measure whether confidence scores rank correct answers above incorrect answers, with higher values preferred.

canonical_statement: AURC was used to summarize average error rate as coverage increases, with lower values preferred and confidence ties averaged analytically.
The default calibration estimator was equal-width 10-bin ECE, with KDE-ECE, KS-Cal, and Smoothed ECE as estimator checks; matched-row comparisons used paired nonparametric bootstrap intervals.

The supplied-answer diagnostic presented canonical gold, plausible wrong, off-type wrong, and re-supplied model answers after Guess: and generated only Probability: to test answer-content sensitivity.

canonical_statement: The main experiments are limited to English short-answer QA and three open 7-8B Instruct models; they do not cover closed systems, broad model-family scaling, long-form generation, multi-turn dialogue, code, or tool use.

The main design teacher-forces an answer generated by the confidence prompt into a counterfactual bare context, so it isolates scoring of one fixed answer rather than comparing two end-to-end prompting systems.
The primary context contrast changes instruction text, chat-turn boundary, and answer marker together and therefore does not identify a single causal prompt token.
Verbalized elicitation is held to one primary decimal-probability template; few-shot calibration, self-consistency, or explanation-before-confidence prompting were not systematically tested.
The protocol audit is a targeted 12-study included sample rated by one author, so it establishes divergence within that set but does not estimate field-wide prevalence.
ECE, AUROC, and AURC evaluate reliability, discrimination, and selective risk but do not establish that either signal is a coherent epistemic or aleatoric uncertainty measure.

The study does not claim that verbalized or token confidence signals are uninformative; its narrower claim is that their values and ordering respond to measurement choices that leave correctness unchanged.

source_anchor.paragraph: Limitations — What we do not claim

canonical_statement: The authors report providing inference and analysis code, prompts, the confidence parser, and supplied-answer inputs, but not generated token-probability outputs; reproducing token probabilities requires rerunning the listed models.

The study concludes that the apparent ordering of verbalized confidence versus token likelihood describes the measurement protocol as much as the model when answer, context, readout, or evaluation choices are left unspecified.
